items.title: Jordan Rossi: “Joy Is Political in Its Own Way”
items.content:
Jordan Rossi has always walked a fine line. British with Italian and Irish roots, he shoots the London queer scene and luxury brand campaigns with equal conviction, never appearing to betray either. His gaze turns fashion photography — vivid, often irreverent — into a tool for intimate and social portraiture. With a single obsession: catching the moment his subjects drop the mask.

The title of your first exhibition, “Homecoming”, speaks of both return and belonging. What does that word mean to you?

Jordan Rossi: “Homecoming” felt like the only possible title. I grew up between two cultures, Italian and Irish, but I was born and raised in London — so I’ve always had a slightly complicated relationship with the idea of “home”. I don’t think I’ve ever felt entirely one thing or another.

Bringing this body of work to Italy feels like closing a circle. These photographs cover nearly a decade of my life, made in London, Los Angeles and elsewhere. Bringing them here, to a country that is part of my identity and my family, feels very personal. But with time, “home” has become less geographical for me. It’s the people you surround yourself with, the communities you find, and eventually the space you create for yourself. In that sense, “Homecoming” is as much about where I am now as it is about where I came from.


You have shot the queer community of East London just as much as campaigns for Rolls-Royce. Are these two worlds not in conflict, and how do you move between them?

Jordan Rossi: I’ve never really seen them as being in conflict. The scale, budgets and expectations might be completely different, but ultimately I’m still interested in the same things: people, character, and creating a world around them.

I also don’t think queer artists should have to exist solely within queer spaces. I can photograph someone in a club in East London and then direct a campaign for a global brand — both can still contain my point of view. If anything, moving between those worlds matters to me. The experiences and communities that shaped me inevitably find their way into the commercial work, and the resources of the commercial world feed back into my personal work. I don’t want either side of my career to exist in isolation from the other.

Your photography is generally described as queer, committed, rooted in fashion and portraiture. What would you add about your work and where it has taken you?

Jordan Rossi: I’d probably add that there’s a sense of performance running through a lot of it. I’m interested in the version of ourselves that we construct for the camera: fashion, sexuality, masculinity, femininity, celebrity, glamour. Portraiture can document somebody, but it can also give them permission to become something else for a moment.

Over the past decade that has taken me into very different rooms — from emerging performers and people within the queer community to actors, musicians, fashion houses and global brands. I’ve photographed people I admired long before I ever picked up a camera professionally, which still feels slightly surreal. But when I look across the work now, what interests me isn’t necessarily who is famous and who isn’t. It’s that the same curiosity runs through all of it. I’m drawn to people who have a strong sense of who they are — or who are in the process of discovering it.


You are a photographer, a filmmaker and a creative director all at once. Concretely, how do you hold those three roles together?

Jordan Rossi: What I’ve realised over time is that every time I’ve added another discipline, it has changed the way I approach everything else.

There are instincts and skills that move between them. Photography made me much more aware of the relationship you build with the person in front of your camera. It can be incredibly intimate — just two people trying to find something together. Learning how to create that trust changed the way I worked with performers when I returned to directing. In the same way, years of filmmaking and creative direction have made me think differently about still images. I’m rarely just thinking about whether something looks beautiful; I’m thinking about the world around it, the character, the emotion, and what the image is trying to say.

That’s ultimately how I hold all three together: they’ve become part of the same visual language. I’m constantly taking things I’ve learned in one area into another, often without consciously realizing it. I’m less interested now in whether something makes me a photographer, director or creative director — and more interested in finding the best way to tell the story in front of me.

In your work, you have chosen to show the joy of the LGBTQIA+ community rather than its trauma. Do you feel a particular responsibility towards that community — and if so, what does it look like?

Jordan Rossi: Absolutely — although I try not to let that responsibility turn into the idea that there is one correct way to represent a community as enormous and varied as ours.

For a long time, so many LGBTQIA+ stories were framed through tragedy, rejection or suffering. Those stories are real and important, but they aren’t the entirety of queer life. I became much more interested in photographing the other side of it: friendship, sex, humor, beauty, ridiculousness, confidence, intimacy and joy. Not as a denial of the difficult things, but because those things are also political in their own way. There is power in seeing queer people simply having a brilliant time, taking up space, being desired rather than apologising for being there.

My responsibility is really to the people in front of my camera. I want them to feel they have agency in how they’re represented, and I want the work to come from being part of a community rather than looking at it from the outside. I don’t think my job is to speak for LGBTQIA+ people. It’s to contribute my perspective to a much bigger, messier and more interesting story.

Jordan Rossi’s show “Homecoming” is on view at Galleria Rubin, Milan (Italy), from September 22 to October 3rd, 2026.

items.title_es: Jordan Rossi: “Joy es político en su propia manera”
items.content_es:
Jordan Rossi siempre ha caminado una línea fina. Británico con raíces italianas e irlandesas, él dispara la escena del queer de Londres y campañas de lujo con igual convicción, nunca parece traicionar tampoco. Su mirada convierte la fotografía de moda — vívida, a menudo irreverente— en una herramienta para el retrato íntimo y social. Con una sola obsesión: capturar el momento en que sus sujetos caen la máscara.

El título de su primera exposición, “Homecoming”, habla tanto de regreso como de pertenencia. ¿Qué significa esa palabra para usted?

Jordan Rossi: “Homecoming” se sentía como el único título posible. Crecí entre dos culturas, italiana e irlandesa, pero nací y me crió en Londres, así que siempre he tenido una relación un poco complicada con la idea de “hogar”. No creo que me haya sentido completamente una cosa u otra.

Traer este cuerpo de trabajo a Italia parece cerrar un círculo. Estas fotografías cubren casi una década de mi vida, hecho en Londres, Los Ángeles y otros lugares. Traerlos aquí, a un país que es parte de mi identidad y mi familia, se siente muy personal. Pero con el tiempo, “hogar” se ha vuelto menos geográfico para mí. Es la gente con la que te rodeas, las comunidades que encuentras, y eventualmente el espacio que creas para ti mismo.


Usted ha disparado a la comunidad queer del este de Londres tanto como las campañas para Rolls-Royce. ¿Estos dos mundos no están en conflicto, y cómo se mueve entre ellos?

Jordan Rossi: Nunca los he visto como en conflicto. La escala, los presupuestos y las expectativas pueden ser completamente diferentes, pero en última instancia todavía estoy interesado en las mismas cosas: personas, personajes, y crear un mundo a su alrededor.

También no creo que los artistas queer deben tener que existir únicamente dentro de los espacios de búsqueda. Puedo fotografiar a alguien en un club en el este de Londres y luego dirigir una campaña para una marca global — ambos pueden contener mi punto de vista. Si algo, moverse entre esos mundos me importa. Las experiencias y comunidades que me formaron inevitablemente encuentran su camino hacia el trabajo comercial, y los recursos del mundo comercial se alimentan de nuevo en mi trabajo personal.

Su fotografía se describe generalmente como queer, comprometido, arraigado en la moda y el retrato. ¿Qué añadiría sobre su trabajo y dónde le ha llevado?

Jordan Rossi: Probablemente añadiría que hay una sensación de rendimiento que se ejecuta a través de un montón de ella. Estoy interesado en la versión de nosotros mismos que construimos para la cámara: moda, sexualidad, masculinidad, feminidad, celebridad, glamour. La retrato puede documentar a alguien, pero también puede darles permiso para convertirse en algo más por un momento.

Durante la última década que me ha llevado a salas muy diferentes —de artistas emergentes y personas dentro de la comunidad queer a actores, músicos, casas de moda y marcas globales. He fotografiado a gente que admiro mucho antes de que alguna vez recogiera una cámara profesionalmente, que todavía se siente un poco surrealista. Pero cuando miro a través del trabajo ahora, lo que me interesa no es necesariamente quién es famoso y quién no. Es que la misma curiosidad que se hace.


Usted es un fotógrafo, un cineasta y un director creativo de una vez. Concretamente, ¿cómo mantienes esos tres roles juntos?

Jordan Rossi: Lo que he realizado con el tiempo es que cada vez que he añadido otra disciplina, ha cambiado la forma en que me acerca a todo lo demás.

Hay instintos y habilidades que se mueven entre ellos. La fotografía me hizo mucho más consciente de la relación que construyes con la persona delante de tu cámara. Puede ser increíblemente íntima — sólo dos personas que intentan encontrar algo juntos. Aprender a crear esa confianza cambió la forma en que trabajaba con los intérpretes cuando volví a dirigir. De la misma manera, años de cine y dirección creativa me han hecho pensar de manera diferente en imágenes todavía.

Así es como retengo a los tres juntos: se han convertido en parte del mismo lenguaje visual. Estoy tomando constantemente cosas que he aprendido en un área en otro, a menudo sin darse cuenta conscientemente de ello. Ahora estoy menos interesado en si algo me hace fotógrafo, director o director creativo, y más interesado en encontrar la mejor manera de contar la historia delante de mí.

En su trabajo, usted ha elegido mostrar la alegría de la comunidad LGBTQIA+ en lugar de su trauma. ¿Sientes una responsabilidad particular hacia esa comunidad, y si es así, cómo es?

Jordan Rossi: Absolutamente — aunque trato de no dejar que esa responsabilidad se convierta en la idea de que hay una manera correcta de representar a una comunidad tan enorme y variada como la nuestra.

Durante mucho tiempo, muchas historias LGBTQIA+ fueron enmarcadas por tragedia, rechazo o sufrimiento. Esas historias son reales e importantes, pero no son la totalidad de la vida queer. Me interesé mucho más en fotografiar el otro lado de ella: amistad, sexo, humor, belleza, ridícula, confianza, intimidad y alegría. No como una negación de las cosas difíciles, sino porque esas cosas también son políticas a su manera de ser brillantes.

Mi responsabilidad es realmente para la gente delante de mi cámara. Quiero que sientan que tienen agencia en cómo están representados, y quiero que el trabajo venga de ser parte de una comunidad en lugar de mirarlo desde fuera. No creo que mi trabajo sea hablar por gente LGBTQIA+. Es contribuir mi perspectiva a una historia mucho más grande, más desordenada y más interesante.

El show de Jordan Rossi “Homecoming” está en la vista Galleria Rubin, Milán (Italia), a partir de septiembre 22 al 3 de octubre de 2026.

items.title: Susan kae Grant: Sweet Dreams Are Made of This
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Susan kae Grant: Sweet Dreams Are Made of This

American photographer Susan kae Grant has made dreams her material and her photographic territory. Night Journey, published by MW Editions, is the culmination of a life’s work: a sumptuous and haunting volume, in black and white, crafted with the precision of a haute couturière of the unconscious.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Susan kae Grant.

Susan kae Grant grew up in a small town in Wisconsin. A shy and silent child, she expressed herself by drawing, writing, and making collages. Alfred Hitchcock and Rod Serling, creator of the anthology series The Twilight Zone, served as her compass: “the way they created mystery came through tormented theatrical storytelling.”

Trained in photography at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, she went on to teach photography at Texas Woman’s University for thirty-six years. Her artistic lineage connects her to what critic A.D. Coleman called the “directorial mode” — a photography in which the scene is entirely constructed by the photographer, in the tradition of Duane Michals, master of narrative sequence, and Arthur Tress, explorer of childhood dreams and nightmares.

In the 1990s, Susan kae Grant agreed to have electrodes placed on her body and to be awakened during REM sleep to describe aloud what she had just seen. Listening back to the recordings, she discovered a voice she barely recognized, phrases spoken in an in-between state, neither fully asleep nor truly awake. “I realized that these recordings had been made in a different state of consciousness.” The words murmured in the dark — “She’s Afraid to Stop”, “Something Needs Constant Attention”, “We Act Like We Don’t Know One Another” — would become the titles of her photographs.

In her Dallas studio, Susan kae Grant works with a 4×5 camera fitted with a digital back. Rare in contemporary photography, she never photographs her subjects directly — only the shadows they cast. She layers models, props, and floral wire, repositioning directional lights dozens of times, sometimes over months, for a single image.

This shadow theater summons Murnau’s Nosferatu and German Expressionism as much as Plato’s allegory of the cave. “It’s like being inside a gigantic three-dimensional photogram that I can’t fully see until I’m behind the camera,” she explains. “I strive to design sets with a sense of mystery and ambiguity, to provoke a narrative that raises more questions than it answers.”

The silhouettes that populate her images have no faces. These anonymous bodies fall, embrace, reach toward something just out of frame. As essayist Deborah Willis writes in the book’s opening essay titled Mapping the Dream Terrain, these figures “function less as characters than as vessels for sensation and memory,” inviting the viewer to project their own nights onto the page. “The narratives are a representation of a representation, and they exist only in the imagination.”

Founder of The Black Rose Press since 1976, Susan kae Grant has produced twelve limited-edition artist books, held in the collections of the Getty Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum. Night Journey is their crowning achievement. With its gatefolds, triptychs, and an entire section printed on translucent paper where images layer like strata of memory, the book performs, down to its very design, the logic of the dream.




Night Journey by Susan kae Grant is published by MW Editions and available for $70.

IN IMAGES

Susan kae Grant: Dulces sueños están hechos de esto

American photographer Susan kae Grant has made dreams her material and her photographic territory. Night Journey, published by MW Editions, is the culmination of a life’s work: a sumptuous and haunting volume, in black and white, crafted with the precision of a haute couturière of the unconscious.

Por Guénola Pellen. Fotos de Susan kae Grant.

Susan kae Grant creció en una pequeña ciudad de Wisconsin. Una niña tímida y silenciosa, se expresó dibujando, escribiendo y haciendo collages. Alfred Hitchcock y Rod Serling, creadora de la serie de antologías La Zona de Crepúsculo, servía como su brújula: "la forma en que crearon misterio vino a través de la narración teatral atormentada."

Entrenada en fotografía en la Universidad de Wisconsin-Madison, continuó enseñando fotografía en la Universidad de Texas Woman durante treinta y seis años. Su linaje artístico la conecta con lo que el crítico A.D. Coleman llamó el “modo directorial” — una fotografía en la que la escena está completamente construida por el fotógrafo, en la tradición de Duane Michals, maestro de secuencia narrativa, y Arthur Tress, explorador de y pesadillas.

En los años noventa, Susan kae Grant aceptó tener electrodos colocados en su cuerpo y ser despertados durante el sueño REM para describir en voz alta lo que acababa de ver. Escuchando de nuevo a las grabaciones, descubrió una voz que apenas reconocía, frases pronunciadas en un estado in-entrenado, ni completamente dormido ni verdaderamente despierto. “Me di cuenta que estas grabaciones habían sido hechas en un estado diferente de conciencia.”Ella tiene miedo de parar”, "Algo necesita atención constante”, "Actúamos como si no conociéramos a uno otro” - se convertiría en los títulos de sus fotografías.

En su estudio de Dallas, Susan kae Grant trabaja con una cámara 4×5 equipada con una espalda digital. Rara en fotografía contemporánea, ella nunca fotografia sus temas directamente — sólo las sombras que proyectan capa. Ess modelos, props y alambre floral, reposicionando luces direccionales tienden de veces, a veces durante meses, para una sola imagen.

Este teatro de sombras convoca a Murnau Nosferatu y el expresionismo alemán tanto como la alegoría de Platón de la cueva. “Es como estar dentro de un gigantesco fotograma tridimensional que no puedo ver completamente hasta que estoy detrás de la cámara”, explica. “Me esfuerzo por diseñar conjuntos con un sentido de misterio y ambigüedad, para provocar una narrativa que plantea más preguntas de las que responde”.

Las siluetas que poblan sus imágenes no tienen rostros. Estos cuerpos anónimos caen, abrazan, alcanzan hacia algo justo fuera del marco. Como escribe el ensayista Deborah Willis en el ensayo de apertura del libro titulado Mapping the Dream Terrain, estas figuras “funcionan menos como personajes que como vasos para la sensación y la memoria”, invitando al espectador a proyectar sus propias noches en la página. “Las narraciones son una representación de una representación, y sólo existen en la imaginación”.

Fundador de The Black Rose Press desde 1976, Susan kae Grant ha producido doce libros de artista de edición limitada, celebrados en las colecciones del Museo Getty y el Museo de Arte Fotográfico de Tokio. Viaje nocturno Con sus portadas, trípticos y toda una sección impresa en papel translúcido, donde las imágenes son capas como estratos de memoria, el libro realiza, hasta su propio diseño, la lógica del sueño.

items.title: The Martin Parr Foundation: The Gothic Next Door
items.content:
IN IMAGES

The Martin Parr Foundation: The Gothic Next Door

The Martin Parr Foundation presents “Dark Tales: British Documentary and the Gothic,” an exhibition that reminds the viewer what makes an atmosphere distinctively British: a fondness for dark irony, layered emotional depth, and a passion for the absurd.

 

By Gaia Squarci. Cover Photo by Chris Shaw

Curator Isaac Blease drew the selection from over 5,000 prints in the Foundation’s collection, spanning more than 80 years, from the post-war years to the present. Together they build a haunted, playful narrative that shows photography’s power to visualise fear and fascination — proof, as Blease puts it, of the Gothic principle that horror lives closest to the familiar.

 

Rather than impose a single viewpoint, the show lets atmosphere serve as its thread, moving from historical documentation to domestic unease to class, into the rituals of appearance and respectability, where details of style are always an indicator of a deeper message. Fading industrial towns, claustrophobic interiors, and eerie nocturnal scenes recur throughout, in work by Bill Brandt, Anna Fox, Don McCullin, Lee Miller, Chris Shaw, and many others.

The exhibition “Dark Tales: British Documentary and the Gothic” is on view at the Martin Parr Foundation in Bristol, UK, until December 20.

items.title: Denis Boulze and the Sweet Life of Clichés
items.content:
“Images don’t belong to us. Proust’s madeleine is the same for everyone.” Set as the epigraph of Clichés (in French, the word means both a stereotype and a photograph), Denis Boulze’s line has the candor of a confession slipped backstage, between two takes. The photographer knows the recipe, having served it for years in the pages of Vogue, Silhouette and Milk, for Hermès and JM Weston: a face, a hand, a shaft of light, and the reader’s memory does the rest. A proven recipe. On Roxane Moreau’s podcast Dans le bain, recorded on the evening of his first solo exhibition, Denis Boulze readily speaks of his “candy images.” Sweet, then, and a little guilty.

The taste goes back a long way. The son of a photographer, Denis Boulze started as an intern at 16 at Studio Rouchon in Paris, where he later assisted Sarah Moon, Jan Walter, Sofia and Mauro. A tough school, and a lucky draw. In the acknowledgments, he gives his father his due, the man who passed on to him “a taste for the image” and taught him “to see.” The rest reads like a travel journal, since this “beautiful profession,” he writes, “has always been a pretext for me to travel, meet new people and live experiences that have deeply enriched me.” A craftsman’s courtesy, which also salutes his agent, the formidable Florence Moll, and the printers David Dahan and Luis Escudero, thanks to whom color printing has, as the artist puts it, “today become an essential part of my work.”

So why a book? Weariness? Remorse? A big spring cleaning? On his professional profile, Denis Boulze once let out this cry from the heart: “Help, fashion! Seeing the same photographers, the same stylists, the same models over and over, I’m getting a little bored.” Clichés answers with the simplest gesture: opening the archive boxes, cutting, pasting, layering. The bags, the bottles, the logos evaporate. What remains are bodies, gestures, postures. Claire Luna, winner of the 2025 AICA-France Élisabeth Couturier Prize for art criticism, sees in it, in her opening text, “almost a visual coming out,” and extends the metaphor all the way to the closet: the curtain has risen, “but something still lies coiled.”

What you find inside: 16 faces striped with shadow, 16 hands raised as if to stop traffic, a white dove above a red and orange puddle, starfish clinging to an ear. A moodboard? Almost. Denis Boulze works in diptychs and strips, slipping a tab of red or khaki-green paper between two prints, the way one dog-ears a page in a cookbook. A woman’s profile answers an antique plaster head; two long-necked bottles bathe in a day-for-night blue, a Morandi gone to the movies; a transparent dress floats against black, a dry cleaner’s ghost. The painted lips, for their part, are doubled, like a rubber stamp pressed twice (Blumenfeld and Man Ray have been here before).

The strength of the whole lies in its softness. Everything here belongs to reminiscence, a tune hummed without knowing who wrote it, hence the title Claire Luna chose, “Comme une chanson populaire” (Like a Popular Song). Denis Boulze embraces this shared memory, which he also claims for his series “Portrait de famille” (Family Portrait), made every summer in a former chestnut-drying hut in the Cévennes: a series “very dear to me,” he wrote, “although it is unfinished and will probably remain so forever,” meant to preserve “this parenthesis of our lives which, in my opinion, resembles a gentle poetry.” Clichés shares this slow tempo, like a family album whose members happen to be strangers.

Designed by Line Célo and printed by LONGO in Bolzano, the book has the restraint of a portfolio laid on a table at a festival portfolio review. Generous white space, airy sequences, color used sparingly and all the more precious for it. Some plates read like a catalog of forms, plaster spheres and half-moons in a Bauhaus vein; others keep a touch of glamour that Denis Boulze owns without false modesty. One could see this as a limitation. One could also read it as a form of honesty: the photographer lays out his alphabet, worn letters included, and leaves readers to recognize their own words in it.

Which leaves the question of authorship. To whom does a hand resting on a cheek belong, an eye under makeup, a glass of milk on a dark table? To everyone, answers the epigraph. To whoever looks, the book corrects. Denis Boulze has known this since childhood, and closes his acknowledgments with his father, thanked for a lifelong lesson: “the importance of looking and cultivating my eye.”

Denis Boulze’s Clichés, with a text by Claire Luna, is self-published and available for €40. To buy the book, contact Denis Boulze directly via his Instagram account.

items.title: Two Images Are Better Than One
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Two Images Are Better Than One

In Frozen Features, American photographer and publisher Jason Fulford overlays his negatives at random. From each collision emerges a third image, forging its own syntax.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Jason Fulford.

A knife plunged into a white table, its shadow stretching long as an accusation, and around it, scattered like coins on a counter, watch faces stripped of their hands. Welcome to Frozen Features: a book where every image is already double, where meaning surfaces in the gap, sharp and immediate, before any explanation.

Jason Fulford holds ten thousand digitized negatives, thirty years of images kept in envelopes, boxed, stored in a cabinet. Last year, he began overlaying them at random, two negatives at a time, to see what their meeting might produce. From roughly a thousand pairs generated by chance, he kept a few hundred, then spent two days with Sarah Chaplin Espenon, editor at Loose Joints, whittling them down to fifty-four: purely intuitive work.

Only the combinations that “sing” survive. Charles Goslin, his graphic design professor, used to collect obituaries from The New York Times featuring people who had led double lives, two improbable existences fused into one. He asked his students to distill that duality into a single logo. Jason Fulford never stopped practicing that exercise.

For the photographer, two images placed side by side alter each other: from their encounter emerges an additional layer of meaning. Ferdinand de Saussure, the father of modern linguistics, put it this way: the value of a sign arises not from its own content, but from its difference from all the others.

A man seen from behind paints a madonna in watercolor against the New Mexico sky: without the straight road stretching beneath his brush, without the arid desert around him, the figure is nothing. With it, she becomes an apparition. Jason Fulford forges morphemes, minimal units whose meaning stays suspended, waiting for encounter.

Frozen Features opens with a line from American photographer Barbara Morgan, written in 1942: “Modern life is photomontage. In our thoughts and feelings, the images vital to us move together, skipping over the factual detail.” Jason Fulford takes her at her word, then goes further: he surrenders syntax to chance in order to surface the grammar buried beneath conscious thought. 

TThese photographs each existed independently, made across thirty years of practice, yet were never intended to meet. In his address to the reader, Jason Fulford writes: “A metaphysical slot machine scoured my subconscious & fed it back to me, two memories at a time.” A fragmented face in a rearview mirror while a freight train barrels past in the background: two moments that never crossed paths now share the same second, and time ceases to be chronological. It becomes stratigraphic.

“The only way for them to last is for them to never fully be resolved,” says Jason Fulford — and one thinks of what American art historian Benjamin Buchloh wrote about Gerhard Richter’s paintings: vexations, puzzles that seem to promise a solution yet resist every attempt to reach one.

Roland Barthes, the French theorist of the image and founding father of modern semiology, called punctum that detail which pricks in a photograph and wounds, in the literal sense: a puncture, a breach in the gaze. Jason Fulford makes images with a double punctum: a toy dinosaur skeleton dissolving into the pink facade of a building at night, two simultaneous wounds contaminating each other. It is, as Loose Joints puts it, work that is “felt before it’s understood.”

Jason Fulford puts it plainly: “I always try to make work that the reader finishes.” And so Frozen Features is not a closed book: it is a half-written score, a sentence missing its verb. This is where the reader comes in. Two images are better than one, granted. But two images plus a gaze: that’s a complete sentence. Yours to make.

 

Frozen Features by Jason Fulford is published by Loose Joints, 104 pages, 54 color plates, $68.

items.title: Black Cowboys Are Back in the Arena
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Black Cowboys Are Back in the Arena

Two years after the success of Eight Seconds: Black Rodeo Culture, Damiani releases a new edition featuring 91 previously unpublished photographs, with a foreword by James Pickens Jr., Grey’s Anatomy actor and rodeo devotee.

 

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Ivan McClellan.

Present on the ranches of the American West since the end of the Civil War, where they made up no less than a quarter of the workforce, Black cowboys have long been rendered invisible by Hollywood and the American national myth. A distortion that photographer Ivan McClellan has been dismantling for ten years, from the dusty arenas of Oklahoma to the red clay lands of Texas.

“We see the faces. The joy. The color. The pageantry. The fellowship. We witness triumph and pain, history and legacy — but above all, celebration,” writes Pickens Jr., an avid rider and organiser of team roping events across Southern California. “This is a Western lifestyle uniquely shaped by the Black cowboy and cowgirl experience.”

“It showed me how vital the Black cowboy’s story is to the true history — and mythology — of the American West,” writes Pickens Jr. in Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion, recalling his first Black rodeo in New York City forty years ago. “That experience changed my perspective. It reshaped my understanding of what it really means to be a cowboy.” It took a photographer from Portland to give the American West back its true color.




Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion by Ivan McClellan. Foreword by James Pickens Jr. Damiani Books, 112 pages, 91 color photographs. $50

items.title: Ai Huang: Personal Development
items.content:
One night in 2021, in Tokyo, Ai Huang pushed aside the curtain of a darkroom for the first time. She emerged at dawn, arms full of distorted portraits, her skin still carrying the sharp smell of developer and fixer. The following night, she came back to make more prints. And the night after. “The faces I created, floating in the water, made me feel less alone.”

What she discovers there at 20, freshly arrived from Philadelphia where she had been studying film, goes far beyond technique. In the chemical baths, she finds an entirely new bodily language: working directly on photographic paper and large-format negatives, she drags developer and fixer across the surface with her bare hands, her fingers, sometimes her hair, coaxing images of rare organic power into being. “The gestures in the chemical baths, the pressure of the body, the passage of time — everything leaves a mark.” She lets the chemicals disobey, steers the accidents. “I’m not trying to control the outcome entirely, but to create the conditions for an encounter. I work in that space where I am both in control and controlled.”

Masato Seto, Japanese-Thai photographer and founder of the gallery-laboratory Place M in Shinjuku, introduced her to Tokyo’s photography scene. He had spotted her after finding a small drawing she had made on the back of a receipt, discarded in a bin, and contacted her the next day to offer her a solo show. “When I went to see him, he had framed that crumpled receipt,” she recalls. “He gave me space, materials, knowledge, and a form of trust that was essential.” The darkroom at Place M became her world: “An intimate space, almost secret, separated from reality by a simple curtain. I felt both vulnerable and free there.” 

Through Seto, she met the great figures of postwar Japanese photography: Masahisa Fukase, author of the legendary Ravens; the towering Daido Moriyama, co-founder of Place M; and Hiroh Kikai, solitary portraitist of the Asakusa district. Eikoh Hosoe — a guiding presence of the Japanese avant-garde of the 1960s, known for his collaborations with writer Yukio Mishima — gave her a set of expired large-format negatives, a gesture that opened an entirely new dimension in her practice.

From this inheritance, the series “KABRALA” was born, now on show for the first time in France at Galerie La Lison, embedded within the tattoo studio La Bête Humaine, where Valérie Dufour has built a space for artists who operate outside institutional circuits, at the crossroads of photography and contemporary art.

The resulting prints are self-portraits, but with no interest in likeness. Faces surface, dissolve, hollow out, burn white with light. Some call to mind funerary masks; others, skins in the process of shedding. Sensuality moves through the very material of the paper — in the rivulets, the fingerprints, the chemical scorches. “Ai Huang does not show herself,” writes Valérie Dufour in her accompanying text. “She commits. Identity appears here as unstable, fragmentary, in motion.”

In 2023 already, at the Kiyosato Museum of Photographic Arts in Japan, she presented a public demonstration of her process, claiming it outright as performance. “The work begins the moment my body comes into contact with the chemicals. What happens next depends on that encounter, and the final image is its trace.” A trace that is singular, corrosive, but alive.

Ai Huang’s exhibition “KABRALA” is on view at Galerie La Lison until October 10, 2026.
items.excerpt: Paris’s Galerie La Lison is hosting the first French solo exhibition of Ai Huang, a Tokyo-based artist whose work explores portraiture through the gelatin silver process — self-portraits of rare intensity, transformed by a radical manipulation of photographic chemistry.

items.title: Cheyco Leidmann: the Red That Bleeds, the Gold That Burns
items.content:
He was six years old. He was handed a Bolex 8mm camera, complete with its full editing kit, the way other children are given a ball or a bicycle. “I was immediately fascinated by moving images, and by the manipulation of those images through editing,” Cheyco Leidmann recalls. He cites Orson Welles and Touch of Evil, a film that “branded him.” Listening to him, it becomes clear that everything starts there: in the early conviction that an image never really tells the truth.

Cheyco Leidmann has never presented himself as a photographer. “These aren’t photos,” he was already correcting people in 1998. “Anyone can be a photographer these days, even with a phone. No, these are images. They’re worked.” It has to be understood this way: no Photoshop, no editing, everything shot on slide film, everything done in the camera. A red, ketchup-colored ice cream, a California license plate reading “FOXY LADY,” a green latex-gloved hand gripping a Cadillac hood. For him, genuine artistic value is the product of meticulous, almost surgical work, the point where glamour, provocation and art collide.

There is something of Nadar in this way of building a myth before the work itself, something of Kerouac in the American road he never stopped traveling, Downtown LA, Soda Lake, Fort Lauderdale, and a touch of Buñuel in these bodies that emerge from cars like surrealist apparitions. He himself prefers to cite Hunter S. Thompson. “One of my favorite books is Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas,” he confides. Reading him, it is no longer surprising that his world resembles a hallucinated road trip in which advertising has seized power.

Foxy Lady was published right in the fertile years of the 1980s and became an instant cult object, sold out, reissued, copied to the point of exhaustion. “My style got copied, admired, criticized and, worse still, my images were stolen,” he said of his 2018 collaboration with stylist Adam Selman. “These are individuals who use other people’s ideas because they are too poor to create something of their own.” The line lands hard.

His longtime creative partner is Ypsitylla von Nazareth, stylist and muse, present since Foxy Lady through his most recent campaigns. “She has taken charge of every production process that followed, right up to today,” he says of her, with the same economy of words he reserves for what truly matters.

From California light, Leidmann shifted one day toward darker visions, the series Toxytt, its fragments, its frontal violence. The shift is surprising, given how opposed the two worlds seem, yet he speaks of it with the same quiet nonchalance. Asked about any regrets, he first deflects, “I am completely low tech,” before delivering the line that sums up his entire system: “I do not try to find out what technique you use to eat.” People inevitably read provocation into it. He defends himself with the same economy of words: “Provoking for the sake of provoking is like buying a ticket to your own concert: it is pointless. It is simply what I feel.”

Then there is the question of the gesture itself, of what happens in the instant of the shutter click. On the secret of the perfect frame: “The eyes are the weapon. You have to think subversively. It all comes down to speed, experience, discipline, reaction, precision and luck, all coming together in a moment of nihilistic silence,” he told Dazed. A few words later, he adds that under these conditions, nine shots out of ten come out right. He is to be believed.

Art? He calls the word “unpleasant, inflationary, a sticker, a price tag, a tool of manipulation.” Cheyco Leidmann thinks as he pleases, lives as he pleases, wherever he pleases, Paris, New York, Miami, Los Angeles, never settling anywhere. “I consider myself a restless, cosmopolitan man,” he says, “I live where I like to live, in Toxytt City,” a city of his own invention, entirely fabricated yet entirely believable, much like his photographs. At YellowKorner, the series “Foxy Lady” and “Silicon” hold the two ends of this America: chrome-plated California on one side, humid Florida on the other. The colors have not shifted a shade.

items.title: Downtown, Behind the Scenes of the City
items.content:
Armed with his film Leica, Alexis Duclos roams the city in search of the unexpected. Where his first exhibition, “En Ville” (“In the City”), captured the poetry of Parisian streets, “Downtown” extends his gaze to other horizons. He builds a monochrome series with a vibrant grain, in which black and white contrasts make light the guiding thread of this urban wandering. The sun rises and floods a Parisian facade, blazes over a Tokyo boulevard at its zenith, then its last rays timidly caress a New York building: across 20 photographs, the exhibition itself becomes a wandering that mirrors the photographer’s own.

We move from one metropolis to another without transition, carried by the same invisible thread linking streets across the world. In the end, it hardly matters where an image was taken, since the city rocks us with the same refrain, as if all cities shared a common language that only the eye could reveal.

Larger than life

From the cover image on, Alexis Duclos shows us that the monumental city and ordinary bodies share the same sky. A knee bent like an arch, a hand wrapped around it. Below, a row of curved backs, bare shoulders, legs dangling at the water’s edge, and far in the background, tiny, almost shy, the iron lady watching over Paris. In this oversized foreground, where flesh becomes landscape, we are plunged into the almost indecent intimacy of the framing.

The photographer plays with dimensions, shifting scales, inviting us to look differently. The fairground is transformed into a Hollywood spectacle, where a papier-mâché King Kong, turned silent guardian of a carousel, looms above the crowd, jaws open on a silent roar, reaching an arm toward the sky as if to pluck the silhouettes spinning at the end of their metal cables.

Nothing is ever quite what it seems, and facades sometimes turn into backstage. That is the case with this image, titled Ascension, where the giant shadow of a service staircase unfolds across a metal fence. We see only the staircase’s reflection, a ghostly, projected version, theatrically lit. As if the building were watching itself, and the cast shadow were the only stage where the real spectacle could finally play out. A set worthy of theater or cinema, it is impossible not to think of The Truman Show. One almost expects to see the character, mid-ascent, reach the top, turn to the audience, take one last bow, and deliver a final line: “Good morning, good afternoon, and good night.”

Film photography, a return to the source

For more than twenty years, Alexis Duclos worked at the heart of current events. Starting in 1985, after a stint at Associated Press, he joined the Gamma agency, where he covered conflicts, political news, sports, and major international events. A photographer honored with several awards, he developed a practice marked by the diversity of terrain he explored. In 2005, as photojournalism underwent major upheaval, he decided to leave Gamma to devote himself to independent projects, moving between documentary photography and audiovisual production. Then, over the years, he gradually turned away from reportage to rediscover the simple pleasure of a photography freed from economic and editorial constraints.

Like a flâneur, Alexis Duclos lets himself be guided by chance. He moves forward with no apparent itinerary, attentive to what escapes hurried eyes. For him, photographing means learning to see, frame, and release the shutter at the right moment. His photographic style is distinctive, built on a rigorous composition in which every element finds its place and contributes to the image’s meaning. “I compose with light and framing to express a moment that, I hope, provokes emotions. That’s when a photograph can speak to me, can speak to us. Or not. It’s simple and complex at once.”

The only constraint the photographer imposes on himself is his choice of focal length: a 50mm lens, the one whose rendering comes closest to human eye perception. Alexis Duclos works exclusively on film: “I love black and white film for its grain, its texture, its material quality, and its aesthetic.” In his view, unlike digital photography and artificial intelligence, where images can be recomposed or artificially generated, film embodies a return to a photographic practice grounded in the materiality of the negative, an indisputable sign that a moment truly existed.

Here, implicitly, we find Roland Barthes’s intuition about photography’s indexical power: the image as trace, as proof that something truly was there, in front of the lens, in a light and an instant that will never occur again.

“Downtown,” by Alexis Duclos, is on view at La Caverne D’Art & Miss gallery in Paris, from September 24 to October 24, 2026.

items.title: Baldwin Lee’s Unseen New York
items.content:
Before the South, there was New York. And before the portraits, the vast emptiness of its architectural structures. Born in 1951, Baldwin Lee grew up in Manhattan’s Chinatown. He first studied under Minor White, a presiding figure of contemplative photography, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, before going on to Yale, where Walker Evans’s teaching — Evans being the undisputed reference of American documentary photography — completed the formation of his eye. “I would tell my students that my photography teachers, White and Evans, were the equivalent of having studied with Matisse and Cézanne,” he recalls in an interview with Jessica Bell Brown published in Baldwin Lee (Hunters Point Press, 2022).

After graduating in 1975, he returned again and again to the city of his childhood, a 4×5 view camera on a tripod over his shoulder, moving through Manhattan at dawn, often in winter, when the sidewalks emptied of their inhabitants. “My trips to New York City from New England were an exploration of buildings as organic forms,” the artist confides. “Rather than approaching the work as architectural photography, I saw it as a way of capturing a landscape. It was my first time using a large-format camera. Early in the morning, with no one around, I felt an overwhelming intimacy — as if I were walking through my own private garden.”

His subjects include Wall Street at dawn, Times Square, and the streets and vacant lots of Lower Manhattan where the World Trade Center looms in the distance. Baldwin Lee records a city suspended between neglect and ambition, where remnants of the past remain visible alongside the structures of the new. Worn brick facades, Cadillac Eldorados parked along the curb, the twin towers still new: these images carry the trace of a human presence temporarily absent but not gone. “If the buildings were people it would be acceptable if they did not speak,” he tells Blind. “The silence can be a metaphor for spaces, once occupied, now vacant. The lack of people points to an unfulfilled potential.”


Baldwin Lee went on to teach at Yale, then at the Massachusetts College of Art. In 1982, he moved to Knoxville, Tennessee, where he founded the photography program at the university, which he would lead for more than thirty years. The following year, he embarked on an extensive series of journeys through the American South. Between 1983 and 1989, he made nearly ten thousand photographs, principally of Black communities — a body of work celebrated as a major social testament to rural Black America. “The photographs I made in the South would never have come about without adequate education and awareness: North/South, Black/white, male/female, private/public, poor/rich, powerful/subjugated,” he tells Jessica Bell Brown.

The New York photographs reveal a different but related aspect of Baldwin Lee’s practice. Their careful organization of architectural space and sustained attention to the character of place helped establish the distinctive visual language he would carry into his later work. They demonstrate a sensitivity to form and order, but also to the humanity inscribed in the built environment. His vision of New York is a record of what people made, inhabited, altered, and left behind.

The prints selected for the exhibition present his images at a scale he has never seen before. “No, I have not seen them printed at that scale,” he confides to Blind. “At this large scale the photographs and the viewer have a different relationship. A dialog between the photograph is possible and encouraged. The viewer is now capable of entering the space of the photo making for a more intimate experience.”

The twin towers that dominate several of his images have since vanished from the New York sky. The city Baldwin Lee once photographed as his own private garden no longer exists.

“Baldwin Lee: New York (1975–1979)” is on show at the Howard Greenberg Gallery from September 18, 2026 to October 31, 2026.

A reception with the artist will be held at the Howard Greenberg Gallery on Thursday, September 17, 2026 from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m.

Baldwin Lee is published by Hunters Point Press (2022).

items.title: Will Vogt: “People Are Rarely As Buttoned-Up As They Appear”
items.content:
In America, fortune is often written in the plural of houses. Will Vogt owns three, which have also served as his hunting grounds as a photographer: a home in Corpus Christi, on the Texas Gulf coast; the family ranch, also in Texas; and, in Watch Hill, Rhode Island, the summer house where his family has gathered — and let themselves be photographed — for generations.

The boy he once was grew up elsewhere, in Haverford, Pennsylvania. More drawn to books than to sport, he discovered F. Scott Fitzgerald at boarding school, fell for his hero, Gatsby, and received his first camera not long after. From then on, it was his own world he turned the lens toward.

More than 70,000 images later, Will Vogt is far more than a chronicler of American wealth. His debut, These Americans, published in 2023, sold out. Three years later, Behind the Hedges returns to the same rituals — epic hunts, grand weddings, private society rallies — but the snapshot has given way to something more composed, and the urgency of youth to something more restrained. Interview.


Your previous book, These Americans, caught the moment. Behind the Hedges, your new book, composes it into tableaux. In practical terms, what changed in the way you shoot and sequence images between the two books?

Will Vogt: I’m not sure that the way I shoot changed as much as my material has. The advent of digital photography has also allowed me to capture more detail, which in turn makes larger tableau images possible.

These Americans drew heavily from photographs I took in the 1980s when I was younger and life around me was moving pretty fast. Behind the Hedges returns to many of the same people, places and traditions thirty years later. I’m older as are many of my subjects and as a result the pictures have slowed down a little too.

What did change enormously was my understanding of editing and sequencing. Before working with Jennifer Garza-Cuen on These Americans, I really had no idea how a photography book was put together. I learned that it isn’t a collection of your best photographs. In a book, the individual images have to work together, create a rhythm and tell a story.

In Behind the Hedges, your frame often leans on the natural or built architecture of a setting: a leading line draws the eye toward the façade of Lainston House, table and chairs arranged in the foreground; elsewhere, a swimming pool fills the foreground of the image. What place does aesthetic hold in your work?

Will Vogt: A very important one. I may be documenting something but I still want to make great photographs. I’ve always been conscious of composition, light and the relationship between people and the places they inhabit.

The surroundings are also part of the story. A house, a swimming pool, a shooting field or a dining room tells you something about the people in the photograph before you know anything about them. Sometimes the setting is every bit as important as the people.

In the essay he wrote to accompany These Americans, novelist Jay McInerney, author of Bright Lights, Big City, says “there’s no pane of glass” between you and your subjects. Doesn’t that closeness encroach on the distance a photographer sometimes needs from his subject?

Will Vogt: Familiarity gives me great access, but more than that it allows people to be comfortable around me and the camera. That is a tremendous advantage.

I think that is where the photographer has to create his own distance. You’re part of the scene but you’re also removed enough to document it. I’ve been doing that for most of my adult life, so I don’t think about it very consciously anymore.


One photograph in Behind the Hedges shows nothing but the filthy window of a Range Rover, finger-written with the line: “I wish my wife was as dirty as this.” The gap between a message that crude and a world that buttoned-up seems to delight you, as though you were forever hunting for the grain of sand that might jam the machine…

Will Vogt: I do like that photograph and particularly the contradiction and the humor. I don’t think I’m hunting for something to jam the machine. I’m looking for things that make the picture more complicated and thought-provoking than what you might expect.

There are plenty of preconceived ideas about this world and photographs like that one upset those expectations a little. People are rarely as buttoned-up as they appear. That’s what makes them interesting to photograph.

Behind the Hedges opens on a quote from F. Scott Fitzgerald, as an epigraph, before the first photograph. What place does literature hold in your eye as a photographer?

Will Vogt: I’ve always read a lot and I’m certainly attracted to writers who are good observers of people and social worlds. I fell in love with the writing of F. Scott Fitzgerald as a boy, about the same time I started taking pictures. He understood that wealth and privilege could be both seductive and complicated. I think I have documented some of that in my own work.

When I’m taking a photograph, I’m not thinking about Fitzgerald or trying to make an image look literary. Those connections tend to emerge later. A photograph can contain a whole story without explaining it. In that sense, I suppose photography and literature have quite a lot in common.

Behind the Hedges returns again and again to scenes of killing: a pit of zebra carcasses, partridges hung in neat rows, hares laid out on moss. What do these scenes of slaughter reveal, in your view, about this supposedly well-mannered society?

Will Vogt: I probably wouldn’t use the word slaughter. Hunting has been a large part of my life and of the world I photograph. Those images are part of the reality of it. I don’t see a reason to sanitize that reality by showing the shooting party and leaving out the dead game.

There is also a long tradition surrounding hunting, particularly in England and South Texas. The game, the land, the dogs, the people and the rituals surrounding all of it are connected. I photograph what is there and leave it to the viewer to decide what he or she thinks about it.

The English photographer Martin Parr, who died in December 2025, spent his life photographing the British middle and working classes and their mass leisure — but as an observer, from outside that world, with an eye that was affectionate and often satirical. You do the opposite: you’ve always photographed the American elite you were born into, from the inside. Do you feel any kinship with him nonetheless?

Will Vogt: Absolutely. I have always admired Martin Parr’s work. We came at our subjects from slightly different angles but I think we shared an interest in the small details that tell you something larger about people and the way they live.

Parr was brilliant at noticing things that other people walked right past. His photographs could be funny without simply making fun of people. I hope there is some of that observational quality in my work.


Jennifer Garza-Cuen, the editor of Behind the Hedges, places your work alongside Larry Sultan, Stephen Shore and Tod Papageorge. What did you take from each of them, and what shows up from those influences in your own eye?

Will Vogt: Those three photographers are masters of their craft and I am honored that anyone would mention me in the same sentence with them. Robert Frank was obviously the earliest and most important influence on my work. I have collected photographs and photography books for many years and inevitably some of what I’ve absorbed has become part of the way I see and photograph the world.

If someone opened Behind the Hedges knowing nothing about you and decided it was satire, what would you tell them?

Will Vogt: I’d tell them they are entitled to see it that way. Once you put photographs into the world, you lose control over how people interpret them.

But satire isn’t my intention. I’m not trying to celebrate these people and I’m not trying to ridicule them. I’m recording a world I know and have been part of for my entire life. There is humor in the photographs because there is humor in life. There are also contradictions and occasionally absurdity. I don’t think you have to manufacture any of that. You just have to notice it.

As a teenager, you saw Jimi Hendrix live — a world at the opposite end of the one you’ve been photographing ever since. You also cite the Beatles and Bob Dylan among your influences. Doesn’t that irreverent spirit find its extension in the way you photograph high society — as a bit of a troublemaker yourself?

Will Vogt: I like the idea of being a troublemaker, although I’m not sure I’ve earned the title.

Music was a huge influence on me when I was young and still is. Hendrix, Dylan and the Beatles all arrived at a time when a lot of accepted ideas about how you were supposed to live were being challenged. I was certainly affected by that.

Maybe some of that does show up in the photographs. I’ve never felt any obligation to make this world look the way it might like to see itself. If something is funny, strange, awkward or a little outrageous, I’m probably going to take the picture. Maybe that is my small contribution to troublemaking.

“Will Vogt: These Americans” runs through December 6, 2026 at the Art Museum of South Texas.

Behind the Hedges (2026), photographs by Will Vogt, edited and with text by Jennifer Garza-Cuen, is published by Schilt Publishing.

These Americans (2023) by Will Vogt is published by Schilt Publishing.

items.title: Stacy Kranitz: A Picture Is Worth a Thousand Wounds
items.content:
“I don’t believe in ending stories. I just don’t do it.” Stacy Kranitz drops the line by Lake Geneva, on the afternoon of the Images Vevey Book Award ceremony, between two questions about swimming. Seventeen years she has been working in Appalachia, the mountain range that runs more than 3,000 kilometers from Canada down to Alabama. Or twenty, she hesitates. The book takes its title from a gospel song by Brother Claude Ely, a Pentecostal preacher from those mountains. The jury chaired by Rineke Dijkstra crowned it; Éditions Images Vevey and the American publisher Terrible Baby brought it out in June. One idea governs the whole: every image manufactures a little of the reputation it claims to describe.

At the Musée Jenisch, the installation applies that principle to the letter. Stacy Kranitz’s color photographs, made in a West Virginia hollow, face the images produced about the region by outsiders since 1850. Missionaries raising funds, photographers on the payroll of the coal companies, envoys of the Farm Security Administration, reporters covering the War on Poverty: each wave arrived with its commission in hand and its framing already written. And a documentary film directed by the photographer holds the center of the display. “There’s no visual literacy in America,” she says. “Nobody knows, understands, or processes how images circulate in the world, the different kinds of apparatuses that are at play. Nobody thinks about this stuff.”

It all starts on a Friday night in 2013, in West Columbia, West Virginia. Stacy Kranitz is invited for a beer at the home of a man who, within the hour, gets into three fistfights, throws chairs and punches his friend Dozer in the face. On the back of his neck, a tattoo: “Honkey.” The lawyer Harry Caudill would have filed Pat Greene among what he called the “dullards” of the back hollows. The photographer, for her part, keeps coming back for a decade, then another. “To me, he really identifies as a mountaineer,” she says of her host. “He really embodies the idea of living mountain life.”

One late summer, on a strip mine reclaimed as an ATV trail, Stacy Kranitz climbs on behind Dozer, camera on her back, after a dozen beers for him. The caption of one picture in the book says the rest: “Stacy and Dozer on his four-wheeler, the moment before it flipped.” Dozer, 95 kilos, lands on her; the quad, 340 kilos, lands on Dozer. One bruised elbow. Back at Pat’s, someone hands her a crushed Lortab to snort for the pain. Participant as much as observer, she photographs from inside the circle, with the risks that implies and the standing it earns.

Then comes the long history, the one the book unfolds through documents. Families left Europe to escape a class system, found themselves indentured, climbed into the mountains and lived a century outside capitalism. Then coal climbed up after them. “They literally stole the land,” Stacy Kranitz says. “They didn’t know they needed to have deeds. Nobody told them they need to have deeds. So who decides that they need to have deeds? The coal companies.” On April 24, 1964, Lyndon Johnson sat on the porch of Tom Fletcher, an unemployed miner in Inez, Kentucky, who had earned about 400 dollars the previous year. The picture became the emblem of the War on Poverty. Fletcher died poor in 2004, worn out by the reporters who came back every ten years to ask whether he still was. At the end of the volume, a “lexicon of dispossession” lines up the words coined to keep these people outside the human contract, from waste people to trailer trash. Four centuries of vocabulary, a single function.

Then there is Harry Caudill, the dark heart of the affair and the subject of the film. His essay “The Rape of the Appalachians,” published in The Atlantic in 1962, and Night Comes to the Cumberlands a year later, turned America’s attention to a region bled dry by coal. Twenty years on, the same man explained poverty by genetics, invited the eugenicist William Shockley to his Kentucky home and floated cash bounties for sterilization. Stacy Kranitz unearthed the footage in which he makes that claim on camera. On November 29, 1990, facing Pine Mountain, Caudill shot himself; his farewell letter is reproduced in the book. One detail from the same archive amuses his Swiss publishers. “He mentions the Swiss. He says, we want to do it like the Swiss,” the photographer reports. The film, for its part, turns back on its own author and asks the question that holds for the entire project: what does an image of poverty do, once it is loose in the world?

Next comes J. D. Vance, whose Hillbilly Elegy (2016) recounts an Appalachian childhood and hands his own people the blame for their decline. Stacy Kranitz places the two men in the same frame and notes the coincidence: Pat’s daughter was taken by child protective services just as Vance was named running mate. “It’s my form of politics,” she says of that montage. “I don’t know why we’re not talking about eugenics more. We are still lurking in that conversation in every direction.” A Nieman Fellow, she is spending the year at Harvard, where she studies eugenics and pronatalism.

The book saves its most troubling object for last. In 2016, a photograph of Pat shirtless in his yard became a meme: “Poor southern conservatives have been voting Republican for generations. And they’re still poor.” Pat, with a criminal record, cannot vote. The essayist Whitney Phillips devotes one of the book’s texts to it. Stacy Kranitz has known the mechanism since 2012, when CNN ran her images of a Pentecostal snake handler and a Ku Klux Klan gathering under the headline “Everyday life in Appalachia.” It took a week on the phone to get the headline changed. “Photography has done a lot of harm to that region,” she says. “That doesn’t mean that you can’t or shouldn’t.” She describes the model that governs the news: “A flood, an earthquake, some disaster, we descend on the region, everyone’s there at the same time, and then we abandon ship.” Her work does the opposite, slowly. “Art allowed me to slow down and tell the story over a much longer period of time. You can’t really do it in journalism.”

So she stays. Stacy Kranitz went through every caption with Pat Greene, recorder on the table. “I really needed him to see what I wrote,” she says, “to make sure that he agreed with the context, with the way that it was being used in the book.” The last pictures date from March 2026. As the book went to press, Pat was in jail, with no one to post bail. “We love to put poor people in jail for no good reason,” she says. Five weeks of silence, then a rehab center, where she was able to visit him. “I’ve never seen him more contemplative,” says the photographer, who has always known him in survival mode. The book ends in the dark; life has turned since. Such is the advantage of stories that keep going. “I will probably be there for a long time, and I will not be leaving.”

Ain’t No Grave Gonna Hold My Body Down by Stacy Kranitz is published by Terrible Baby / Éditions Images Vevey and available for $70. The exhibition at the Musée Jenisch, part of the Images Vevey Biennial, runs through September 27, 2026.

items.title: Vic Bakin: Fading
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Vic Bakin: Fading

In Materia, his second book following the monograph Epitome, Kyiv-based photographer Vic Bakin sets images against the decay of their own physical support.

 

By Gaia Squarci. Photographs by Vic Bakin

This work began with two portraits of the same man, made ten years apart. Bakin printed these and other portraits, together with interiors and details hinting at lingering moments, on discontinued photographic paper from the 1960s to the 2000s. Each batch aged differently: faded, spotted with mold or marked by fingerprints.

The paper’s decay seems to mirror the vulnerability of the skin. Fragility, desire, and the relentless pull of time all surface from the same image. As Bakin puts it: “For me, thinking happens through making. I rarely begin with a clear concept. Instead, I make pictures first and then spend months trying to understand what they are telling me.”

The book Materia is published by VOID and available for 60 Euro.
